The severity will depend on the extent of mining, the quantity of runoff, and the flow conditions. Chemical and sediment inputs to local creeks will cause concentrations of these constituents to be higher than what are presently observed. Unavoidable adverse impacts on the quality of surface water are highly speculative since drainage from affected areas will be impounded until water quality criteria are satisfied. Runoff sufficient to exceed sediment pond capacity would result in the uncontrolled discharge of water, but the volume of water involved would dilute chemical contaminants to a large extent. During such an event, increases in suspended sediments from mined areas would result. Quantities of sediment which would be carried downstream are difficult to project, since a relatively small percentage of the area will be unvegetated at any one time. With a maximum of about 2,750 acres to be in a disturbed condition at any one time at the projected or low level of development, and assuming (1) a 100 percent increase in sediment yield from disturbed areas, (2) all disturbance located within the Sarpy Creek drainage, and (3) sustained runoff in excess of sediment pond capacity, the increases in suspended sediment at the confluence of Sarpy and East Sarpy Creeks and at the mouth of Sarpy Creek would be 2.7 percent and .9 percent, respectively. At the high level of production and utilizing the preceding assumptions the increases in suspended sediments at the confluence of Sarpy and East Sarpy Creeks and at the mouth of Sarpy Creek would be 4.0 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively.
